claims.text: The factors of production are the inputs used together to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Each factor of production earns a reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, and enterprise earns profit.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Land is a natural resource supplied by nature, whereas capital is a man-made input produced to aid production; the test that separates them is origin, not cost - a borehole pump is capital while the aquifer it taps is land.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Mobility of a factor of production is the ease with which it moves between one use and another, called occupational mobility, or between one place and another, called geographical mobility.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Labour mobility tends to be held back by specific skills that do not transfer, the cost and time of retraining, housing costs and family ties, so workers can remain unemployed in one town while vacancies sit unfilled in another.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Retraining raises the occupational mobility of workers, and moving house raises their geographical mobility, so a worker who retrains or relocates can take work that was out of reach before.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The quantity of a factor of production is how much of it is available, counted in units such as workers or hectares, while its quality is how productive each unit is in use, such as a worker's skill or the fertility of soil.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Raising the quality of a factor raises the output each unit produces, so output can grow without any increase in the quantity of the factor, as when trained machinists produce more shirts per worker on the same machines.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An economy can raise output either by adding units of a factor or by improving the productivity of the units it already has, and the quality route tends to suit economies whose workers are already numerous.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
